issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette:
For as long as he could remember, Duy had been a man who kept things orderly. At fifty-one, working as a tax inspector for the state, he spent his days in a windowless cubicle reviewing spreadsheets and flagging discrepancies, a profession that rewarded the very meticulousness he had always prided himself on. But order, he had learned, was no protection against what happened in the dark hours of a Tuesday night three years ago.

His wife, Linh, had come home late from a dinner with friends. Duy had asked a simple question—whether she had remembered to file the quarterly estimate—and something in her face had shifted. What followed was a blur, a series of jagged fragments that he could never quite assemble into a coherent whole. He remembered the sting of her open palm against his cheek, the shock that froze him in place. He remembered the heel of her shoe connecting with his ribs as he curled on the kitchen floor. And then, nothing. A gap. A black hole where the next several minutes should have been. He had woken on the tile, alone, with a sharp pain in his side and the taste of blood in his mouth. He never called the police. He never told a soul. He simply got up, cleaned the floor, and went to bed.

In the months that followed, the memory did not stay buried. It forced its way into his mind at the worst moments—while he was driving, while he was trying to focus on a client’s return, while he was lying beside Linh in the dark. The fragments came without warning: the cold tile against his cheek, the sound of her voice, the smell of the dinner she had brought home. Then, just as suddenly, they vanished, leaving him disoriented and ashamed. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The world felt flat, drained of possibility. He moved through his days like an object being pushed from task to task, a thing rather than a person. The betrayal was the worst part. He had trusted Linh completely, had built his life around her, and she had broken something fundamental. He was certain now that trust was a trap.

The symptoms bled into every corner of his existence. At work, he began to feel uncomfortable in the open bullpen, exposed and watched. He started arriving early to claim the desk with its back to the wall, and if someone took it first, he would feel a spike of panic so sharp that he would retreat to the bathroom until his heart slowed. He found himself checking over his shoulder whenever he walked to the parking garage, certain that someone was following him even though he knew, rationally, that no one was. At home, unpredictable situations—a sudden knock at the door, Linh’s voice raised on the phone—sent him into a state of hypervigilance. He reacted as if he were in danger even when nothing was wrong, his body bracing for a blow that never came.

Fatigue became his constant companion. The exhaustion was not physical so much as total, a bone-deep weariness that made the simplest tasks feel monumental. He stopped meeting his colleagues for lunch, stopped attending his son’s weekend soccer games. He told himself it was because he needed rest, but the truth was that he could not bear the unpredictability of other people—their moods, their movements, their unspoken expectations. He had begun to feel unsafe unless his back was against a wall and he could see the entire room. The consequence was a slow, grinding isolation. His supervisor had pulled him aside twice to ask if everything was all right; Duy had smiled and said he was just tired.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not the fear, nor the exhaustion, nor the memory gaps that still haunted him. It was a single moment, three weeks ago, when his son had asked him to play catch in the backyard. Duy had felt his chest tighten, his throat close. He had said no, and had seen the boy’s face fall. That night, lying awake, he had realized that he was disappearing from his own life. He was terrified of what might happen if he let himself feel the full weight of what Linh had done, but he was even more afraid of what he was becoming—a ghost in his own home. He did not know if he could be put back together, but he had come here, to this room, because he had nowhere else to go.
